lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: This is Wild Multiverse. Nature documentaries about creatures that are, frankly, too much.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Wild Multiverse. One oh four point eight. Very quietly now.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Wild Multiverse. Broadcasting from a very long way from a road.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Good morning, from the tall grass. This is Wild Multiverse. Something enormous is waking up.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Wild Multiverse, by night. Keep your voice down. Keep your feet inside the tent.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: You're listening to Wild Multiverse.

lines.speaker: Pip (Camera)
lines.text: Sir Reginald. It's behind you.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Of course it is.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Wild Multiverse. Please do not feed the crew.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Here, in the tall grass, we find one of the multiverse's most patient creatures. The mostly-neck giraffe.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: It began walking past our camera at dawn. It is now mid-afternoon. We have seen the legs. We have seen the first eleven miles of neck. We have not yet seen the head.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Some say the head is in another weather system. Some say there is no head at all, only more neck, curving gently into the upper atmosphere, forever.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Pip, our camera operator, has asked whether we might break for lunch. We may not. The neck continues.

lines.speaker: Pip (Camera)
lines.text: It's been nine hours.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: And what a nine hours they have been.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: At dusk, the coiled spring deer emerges to feed. Each step is a decision. Each decision is a bounce.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: The herd crosses the valley in great slow arcs, never touching the ground for long, as though the ground had once said something unkind.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Here, a young buck attempts his first proper leap. He is overconfident. He has compressed much too far.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: He is gone.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: He is somewhere near the coast now, we believe. He will walk back. It will take him a week. He will have learned nothing. It is, quite simply, magnificent.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Listen. There. And there again. That is the call of the lesser spotted echo, a creature so shy it has never once been seen. Only heard, repeating whatever was said just before.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: For three weeks we have tried to film it. For three weeks it has only repeated our arguments about where to put the camera.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: We have tried playing it birdsong. It played us back our own birdsong, slightly worse. We have tried silence. It has a very good silence.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Then, last night, by the fire, Pip leaned over and whispered to me.

lines.speaker: Pip (Camera)
lines.text: I think I've found it.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: That was not Pip.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: In autumn, the folding elk prepares for winter in the only way it knows. It folds.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: First the antlers. Then the legs. Then, with a sound like someone closing a very old map, everything else. By November, a fully grown bull can be slipped into an envelope.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Many are. Some are posted to relatives. In spring, they unfold wherever they happen to have landed, blinking, in sorting offices across the continent, with no idea how to get home.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Postal workers say that an elk unfolding is the single most surprising thing that can happen in a sorting office, narrowly ahead of a letter addressed to them personally.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: And so begins the great migration. On foot. With stamps on.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: The velvet tortoise is the slowest romantic in the animal kingdom.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: This male began his courtship display in the spring of last year. He has now completed the first part. He has raised one eyebrow.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Across the clearing, the female has noticed. Within the next eighteen months, she may raise one of her own.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: The crew planned to stay for it. Two of them have since married. Not each other. They met other people, in the time. Life goes on, all around the tortoise. The tortoise does not mind. The tortoise has an eyebrow to attend to.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: The upside-down heron fishes not in the river, but in the sky.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Standing on the surface of the water, feet perfectly dry, head pointed down, it waits for something to swim past in the clouds below. A swallow. A kite. Very occasionally, a deeply confused aeroplane.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: It is very still for very long stretches, which the crew have found inspiring, and which the heron has found mildly unsettling, as it can see us, upside down, being inspired.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Today it has been lucky. It has caught a small cumulus.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: It does not know what to do with it. Neither, frankly, do we. It is raining on the heron now. The heron looks betrayed.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: As night falls, the hat moth begins its search. It is drawn not to the light, but to hats. Any hat. A bowler. A bonnet. A sun hat left on a bench.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: It lands, and it stays, and that hat becomes its whole life.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Pip has been wearing a woolly hat since Tuesday. There are now, by our count, forty moths on it. He says it is very warm. He says he cannot take it off. He says they hum, at night.

lines.speaker: Pip (Camera)
lines.text: They do hum.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: He is, I think, quite happy.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Beneath these waves lives the bashful leviathan. The largest creature ever recorded, and by some distance the most easily embarrassed.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: It is the length of four cathedrals. If you look at it directly, it turns pink and swims away, causing a small tidal wave.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Its song is a long, low murmur that translates, roughly, as please stop looking. Followed by, are you still looking. Followed by, oh no.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: We have been filming it through our fingers. Even so, it knows. Look.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: It's blushing.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Everybody hold on to something. Pip, hold on to the camera. Pip, the camera is not something to hold on to. Pip.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Across the great plains, the herd thunders. The pocket bison.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Each one is about the size of a teacup, and roughly as calm. Seven thousand of them, stampeding at full speed, sound like somebody gently shaking a box of raisins.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: They migrate twice a year. North for the summer, and then, after some discussion, slightly further north.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: They have no natural predators. Nothing can bring itself to hurt them. Our sound recordist wept for an hour. I have not stopped.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: They are coming this way. They are going up Pip's trouser leg. Stay very still, Pip.

lines.speaker: Pip (Camera)
lines.text: They're so small.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: On the shore at low tide, the humming crabs gather to sing. Nobody knows the song. It is very long, and it changes key whenever a cloud passes over the moon.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: They come in their hundreds, claws raised, eyes closed. The old ones at the front carry the tune. A young one at the back hums slightly sharp. Nobody corrects him. Nobody ever has. That, I think, is what makes it a choir.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Tonight, the crabs are humming something we almost recognise. Listen.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: It goes... da da dum. Da da.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Someone, please. Find Bev.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: The lantern badger lights its own way, with a small glowing patch on its back that it cannot see, and does not know is there.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: It believes the world is simply brighter wherever it happens to go. It is the most optimistic animal we have ever filmed. We did not have the heart to tell it.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: It greets every tree as though the tree had personally arranged to be lit up for the occasion. The trees, to their credit, have never once corrected it.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Look at it now, trotting into the dark wood, absolutely certain that the dark wood is lovely.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: And, to be fair to the badger, wherever it goes, it is.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Here, on the high moor, a rare sight. A wild armchair.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: These creatures roam the uplands alone, grazing on loose change and lost remote controls. Approach slowly. And never, ever sit down. The armchair will accept you, and you will not get up again.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Here we see a mature male, a high-backed wing chair in his prime. Note the lace doily on the headrest. That is a display feature. It means he is ready to be sat in.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Pip sat down at half past two.

lines.speaker: Pip (Camera)
lines.text: It's extraordinarily comfortable.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: He says he understands now. He has asked us to go on without him. We will send a postcard.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: And now, something I never expected to film. A shadow. On its own. No owner.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: It moves through the grass at sunset, stretching long, then short, then long again, as if trying on different sizes. Locals call him Greg.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: He was attached, once, to someone called Hollis, in a town not far from here. One morning, when Hollis stopped walking, Greg simply kept going. Hollis still leaves the porch light on.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: We followed him for three days. He never once looked back. Although on the second evening, he stopped at a gate and waited a long while, the way you wait for someone who is a little behind you. Then he went on.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: He is the freest thing I have ever seen.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Pip. Don't step on him.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: The common sigh is found in every habitat on earth, from the rainforest to the waiting room. It is almost invisible.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: It feeds on Tuesday afternoons, long queues, and the last biscuit going to someone else. When disturbed, it escapes through the nearest person's nose.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: There are more common sighs in a single office building than there are stars in the sky, and on a Monday morning, the numbers are frankly alarming.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: There.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Just then. You heard it. We all heard it.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: A perfect specimen. Possibly the finest we have recorded. I may have to sit down.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: In the wetlands lives the ladder crane, a bird so tall that it nests on the heads of other birds.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Each spring, the young must make their first descent. It is a long way down, and there are no rungs.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: The parents do not help. They stand on the heads of other birds, looking down, the way all parents look down, hoping, and pretending they are not holding their breath.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: The ladder crane is the only creature in nature ever to be offered a sponsorship deal by Grumbel's Ladders. It declined. It said that up was a choice, and so was falling gracefully.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: And there it goes.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Gracefully.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: Today, a rare encounter with the great crested doubt, a large and pensive bird that feeds on certainty.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: It has been circling our camp since dawn. It has already eaten Pip's confidence, and most of the director's plan.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: This morning it landed on the sound recordist's shoulder, and she spent forty minutes wondering whether she had left the oven on. She has never owned an oven.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: I myself am no longer entirely sure this is a documentary.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: I'm sure it is.

lines.speaker: Sir Reginald Thistlewood
lines.text: I think it is. Remarkable creature. Possibly. I'd like to say remarkable. Pip, is it remarkable?

lines.speaker: Pip (Camera)
lines.text: I don't know any more.
